claim: Equilibrium fluctuations and triggered conformational changes often underlie the functional cycles of membrane proteins.
source: Equilibrium fluctuations and triggered conformational changes often underlie the functional cycles of membrane proteins.
evidence: This is a general statement about membrane protein function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Transporters mediate the passage of molecules across cell membranes by alternating between inward- and outward-facing states.
source: For example, transporters mediate the passage of molecules across cell membranes by alternating between inward- and outward-facing states, while receptors undergo intracellular structural rearrangements that initiate signaling cascades.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about transporter mechanisms.

claim: Receptors undergo intracellular structural rearrangements that initiate signaling cascades.
source: For example, transporters mediate the passage of molecules across cell membranes by alternating between inward- and outward-facing states, while receptors undergo intracellular structural rearrangements that initiate signaling cascades.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about receptor mechanisms.

claim: AlphaFold2 achieved success in CASP14 by modeling a transporter in multiple conformations to high accuracy.
source: Although the conformational plasticity of these proteins has historically posed a challenge for traditional de novo protein structure prediction pipelines, the recent success of AlphaFold2 (AF2) in CASP14 culminated in the modeling of a transporter in multiple conformations to high accuracy.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to CASP14 results and AF2's performance.

claim: AF2 was designed to predict static structures of proteins.
source: Given that AF2 was designed to predict static structures of proteins, it remains unclear if this result represents an underexplored capability to accurately predict multiple conformations and/or structural heterogeneity.
evidence: This statement is based on knowledge of AF2's design objectives.

claim: Reducing the depth of input multiple sequence alignments by stochastic subsampling led to the generation of accurate models in multiple conformations.
source: Whereas models of most proteins generated using the default AF2 pipeline are conformationally homogeneous and nearly identical to one another, reducing the depth of the input multiple sequence alignments by stochastic subsampling led to the generation of accurate models in multiple conformations.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Models generated using the default AF2 pipeline are conformationally homogeneous and nearly identical to one another.
source: Whereas models of most proteins generated using the default AF2 pipeline are conformationally homogeneous and nearly identical to one another, reducing the depth of the input multiple sequence alignments by stochastic subsampling led to the generation of accurate models in multiple conformations.
evidence: This observation is supported by data from the study's experiments.

claim: The conformations generated spanned the range between two experimental structures of interest.
source: In our benchmark, these conformations spanned the range between two experimental structures of interest, with models at the extremes of these conformational distributions observed to be among the most accurate (average template modeling score of 0.94).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from the benchmark study.

claim: Models at the extremes of conformational distributions were among the most accurate with an average template modeling score of 0.94.
source: In our benchmark, these conformations spanned the range between two experimental structures of interest, with models at the extremes of these conformational distributions observed to be among the most accurate (average template modeling score of 0.94).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The vectorial translocation of substrates by transporters is mediated by movements that open and close extra- and intracellular gates.
source: For example, the vectorial translocation of substrates by transporters is mediated by movements that open and close extra- and intracellular gates (Drew and Boudker, 2016; Kazmier et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For GPCRs, ligand binding on the extracellular side triggers structural rearrangements on the intracellular side that initiate downstream signaling.
source: For G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), ligand binding on the extracellular side triggers structural rearrangements on the intracellular side that initiate downstream signaling (Wang et al., 2020; Gusach et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Traditional computational prediction pipelines reliant on inter-residue distance restraints have historically struggled to accurately predict the structures of membrane proteins.
source: Traditional computational prediction pipelines reliant on inter-residue distance restraints calculated from deep multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) have historically struggled to accurately predict the structures of these proteins and their movements.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research documenting these limitations.

claim: AF2 modeled the multidrug transporter LmrP in multiple conformations during CASP14.
source: Upon examining the list of CASP14 targets and corresponding models, we found that AF2 modeled the multidrug transporter LmrP (target T1024) in multiple conformations, two of which were individually consistent with published experimental data (Jumper et al., 2021b; Del Alamo et al., 2021a; Debruycker et al., 2020; Martens et al., 2016; Masureel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to CASP14 results and published experimental data.

claim: Two of the LmrP conformations modeled by AF2 were individually consistent with published experimental data.
source: Upon examining the list of CASP14 targets and corresponding models, we found that AF2 modeled the multidrug transporter LmrP (target T1024) in multiple conformations, two of which were individually consistent with published experimental data (Jumper et al., 2021b; Del Alamo et al., 2021a; Debruycker et al., 2020; Martens et al., 2016; Masureel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published experimental data.

claim: The study was restricted to proteins whose structures were absent from the PDB before April 30, 2018 and have since been determined at atomic resolution in two or more conformations.
source: The neural networks used for prediction were trained on all structures deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) on or before April 30, 2018 (Jumper et al., 2021a). Therefore, by necessity, this study is restricted to proteins whose structures were absent from the PDB before this date and have since been determined at atomic resolution in two or more conformations.
evidence: This describes the study design and selection criteria.

claim: Five transporters were selected that reflected a range of transport mechanisms including rocking-bundle, rocker-switch, and elevator.
source: We selected five transporters that not only met these criteria but also reflected a range of transport mechanisms characterized in the literature (Drew and Boudker, 2016), including rocking-bundle (LAT1, Yan et al., 2019; Yan et al., 2021; ZnT8, Xue et al., 2020), rocker-switch (MCT1, Wang et al., 2021; STP10, Bavnhøj et al., 2021), and elevator (ASCT2, Garibsingh et al., 2021; Garaeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the study design with citations to literature characterizing these mechanisms.

claim: Three GPCRs were included distributed across classes A, B1, and F.
source: We also included three GPCRs, which were distributed across classes A (CGRPR, Liang et al., 2020; Josephs et al., 2021), B1 (PTH1R, Ehrenmann et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2019), and F (FZD7, Xu et al., 2021; to serve as points of comparison, we used the active conformation of FZD7 and the inactive conformation of the nearly identical FZD4, Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the study design with citations to structural data.

claim: Models generated using the default AF2 structure prediction pipeline were largely identical to one another and failed to shed light on the target protein's conformational space.
source: The structures were then predicted using the default AF2 structure prediction pipeline in the absence of templates. However, the resulting models were largely identical to one another and failed to shed light on the target protein's conformational space.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's experimental results.

claim: Reducing the number of recycles to one and restricting the depth of randomly subsampled MSAs to as few as 16 sequences diversified the models generated by AF2.
source: To diversify the models generated by AF2, we reduced the number of recycles to one and restricted the depth of the randomly subsampled MSAs to contain as few as 16 sequences.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: 50 models of each protein were generated for each MSA size.
source: To sample the conformational landscape more exhaustively, we generated 50 models of each protein for each MSA size, while skipping the final MD simulation to reduce the pipeline's total computational cost.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Accurate models of all eight protein targets were obtained for at least one conformation with TM score ≥0.9.
source: Accurate models of all eight protein targets were obtained for at least one conformation (TM score ≥0.9), consistent with published performance statistics (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MSAs with hundreds or thousands of sequences were generally observed to engender tighter clustering in conformations specific to each protein.
source: MSAs with hundreds or thousands of sequences were generally observed to engender tighter clustering in conformations specific to each protein.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data analysis.

claim: Decreasing the depth of the subsampled MSAs appeared to promote the generation of alternative conformations in most proteins.
source: Decreasing the depth of the subsampled MSAs, by contrast, appeared to promote the generation of alternative conformations in most proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments.

claim: The increased diversity from shallow MSAs coincided with the generation of misfolded or outlier models.
source: The increased diversity coincided with the generation of misfolded or outlier models.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data.

claim: Misfolded models virtually never coclustered and could be identified and excluded from further analysis.
source: However, unlike the models of interest that resembled experimentally determined structures, misfolded models virtually never coclustered and could thus be identified and excluded from further analysis (example shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: MCT1 was exclusively modeled by AF2 in either inward-facing or fully occluded conformations.
source: One target, MCT1, was exclusively modeled by AF2 in either inward-facing (IF) or fully occluded conformations; over 99% of the models had TM scores of ≥0.9 and <0.9 to the IF and outward-facing (OF) structures, respectively, regardless of MSA depth.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's data.

claim: Over 99% of MCT1 models had TM scores of ≥0.9 to the IF structure and <0.9 to the OF structure, regardless of MSA depth.
source: One target, MCT1, was exclusively modeled by AF2 in either inward-facing (IF) or fully occluded conformations; over 99% of the models had TM scores of ≥0.9 and <0.9 to the IF and outward-facing (OF) structures, respectively, regardless of MSA depth.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data.

claim: Accurate OF models of MCT1 were obtained only with MSAs containing 16–32 sequences when using OF templates.
source: Therefore, we investigated the effect of providing templates of homologs in exclusively OF conformations alongside MSAs of various sizes (see Methods for details on template selection). Accurate OF models were obtained only with MSAs containing 16–32 sequences and constituted a minor population in an ensemble dominated by IF models.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Both conformations of all eight protein targets could be predicted with AF2 to high accuracy (TM score ≥0.9) by using MSAs that are far shallower than the default.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that both conformations of all eight protein targets could be predicted with AF2 to high accuracy (TM score ≥0.9) by using MSAs that are far shallower than the default.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's data.

claim: The optimal MSA depth and choice of templates varied for each protein.
source: However, because the optimal MSA depth and choice of templates varied for each protein, these parameters need to be explored for conformational sampling of a particular target.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's observations.

claim: Correlation between Cα atom distance between experimental structures and RMSF among models was observed in most cases.
source: To further investigate the structural heterogeneity predicted by these models, we calculated each residue's Cα atom distance between the two superimposed experimental structures, as well as each residue's root mean square fluctuation (RMSF) among all 50 models following structure-based alignment (Figure 2). Correlation between these two measures was observed in most cases and was notable for ASCT2, LAT1, CGRPR, and MCT1 with templates (R2 ≥ 0.75).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: ASCT2, LAT1, CGRPR, and MCT1 with templates showed notable correlation with R2 ≥ 0.75.
source: Correlation between these two measures was observed in most cases and was notable for ASCT2, LAT1, CGRPR, and MCT1 with templates (R2 ≥ 0.75).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The correlation demonstrates that predicted flexibility by AF2 is related to the protein's dynamics inferred from the experimental structures.
source: The correlation demonstrates that predicted flexibility by AF2 is related to the protein's dynamics inferred from the experimental structures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation data.

claim: The predicted flexibility values failed to correlate with their pLDDT values.
source: In contrast with a recent preprint (Saldaño et al., 2021), the predicted flexibility values failed to correlate with their pLDDT values, which reflect the confidence of the AF2 prediction of each residue's local environment (Mariani et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis that contrasts with prior work.

claim: Many of the predicted models fall 'in between' the two experimentally determined conformations.
source: Visual examination suggested that many of the predicted models fall 'in between' the two experimentally determined conformations (example shown in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection of the models.

claim: The first principal component captured 64.9% ± 16.1% of the structural variations among the models generated using MSAs with 32 or more sequences.
source: In our benchmark set, the first principal component (PC1) captured 64.9% ± 16.1% of the structural variations among the models generated using MSAs with 32 or more sequences (Figure 3B), while comparison of PC1/PC2 values suggested that the predicted dynamics deviate from simple interpolation of two end states (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from PCA analysis.

claim: The experimental structures virtually always occupied well-defined extreme positions in the PCA.
source: The experimental structures virtually always occupied well-defined extreme positions.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis.

claim: A correlation was evident between each model's PC1 values and their TM scores.
source: In every case, a correlation was evident between each model's PC1 values and their TM scores.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The models with the most extreme PC1 values were among the most accurate with average TM scores of 0.94 for the top 1, top 3, and top 10 PC1 models.
source: Indeed, the models with the most extreme PC1 values were also among the most accurate: average TM scores were 0.94 for the top 1, top 3, and top 10 PC1 models, and Pearson's correlation coefficients between PC1 and TM scores of the ensemble of models exceeded 0.8 for all transporters in this dataset.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Pearson's correlation coefficients between PC1 and TM scores exceeded 0.8 for all transporters in the dataset.
source: Indeed, the models with the most extreme PC1 values were also among the most accurate: average TM scores were 0.94 for the top 1, top 3, and top 10 PC1 models, and Pearson's correlation coefficients between PC1 and TM scores of the ensemble of models exceeded 0.8 for all transporters in this dataset.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The experimental structures virtually always flanked the AF2 models along PC1.
source: Moreover, the experimental structures virtually always flanked the AF2 models along PC1.
evidence: This is an observation from the PCA analysis.

claim: PTH1R was determined in a partially inactive and active conformation.
source: The exception, PTH1R, was determined in a partially inactive and active conformation (Zhao et al., 2019), suggesting that models extending beyond the former state along PC1 may represent the fully inactive conformation.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to structural data.

claim: Models extending beyond the partially inactive state of PTH1R along PC1 may represent the fully inactive conformation.
source: The exception, PTH1R, was determined in a partially inactive and active conformation (Zhao et al., 2019), suggesting that models extending beyond the former state along PC1 may represent the fully inactive conformation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the PCA results.

claim: Accurate representative models of conformations of interest can be selected from the extreme positions along PC1.
source: Therefore, these results indicate that accurate representative models of conformations of interest can be selected from the extreme positions along PC1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data analysis.

claim: Four membrane proteins with two experimentally determined conformations were investigated, at least one of which was included in the AF2 training set.
source: A follow-up question centers on whether this strategy can yield similar results for proteins with one conformation present in the AF2 training set. We investigated this question using four membrane proteins with two experimentally determined conformations, at least one of which was included in the AF2 training set: the class A GPCR CCR5 (Zheng et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021), the serotonin transporter SERT (Coleman et al., 2016; Coleman et al., 2019), the multidrug transporter PfMATE (Tanaka et al., 2013; Zakrzewska et al., 2019), and the lipid flippase MurJ (Kuk et al., 2017; Kuk et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental design with citations to structural data.

claim: The majority of transporter models generated were more similar to the conformation present in the training set than the conformation absent from the training set.
source: Unlike the results presented above, the majority of the transporter models generated this way were more similar to the conformation present in the training set than the conformation absent from the training set (i.e., their TM scores were greater; Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments on proteins in the training set.

claim: The conformational diversity of models of proteins in the training set was far more limited than what was observed for proteins absent from the training set.
source: The conformational diversity of these models, including those generated using shallow MSAs, was far more limited than what was generally observed for the proteins discussed above, with the exception of MCT1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from the study's data.

claim: None of the models of MurJ and PfMATE adopted the alternative conformer.
source: Although conformational diversity was demonstrated to a limited extent by the generation of occluded models of MurJ and PfMATE, none of the models observed adopted the alternative conformer.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments.

claim: Models of CCR5 were less biased toward the training set conformation, but deep MSAs reduced conformational diversity.
source: By contrast, while models of CCR5 were less biased toward the training set conformation, deep MSAs reduced conformational diversity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments.

claim: The AF2 training set featured the structures of many active GPCRs but no structures of IF MATEs.
source: This divergence in performance may stem from the composition of the AF2 training set, which featured the structures of many active GPCRs but no structures, for example, of IF MATEs (Claxton et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference about the training set composition supported by a citation.

claim: AF2 can be manipulated to accurately model alternative conformations of transporters and GPCRs whose structures were not available in the training set.
source: Our results indicate that the state-of-the-art de novo structural modeling algorithm AF2 can be manipulated to accurately model alternative conformations of transporters and GPCRs whose structures were not available in the training set.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: The use of shallow MSAs was instrumental to obtaining structurally diverse models in most proteins.
source: The use of shallow MSAs was instrumental to obtaining structurally diverse models in most proteins, and in one case (MCT1) accurate modeling of alternative conformations also required the manual curation of template structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Accurate modeling of alternative conformations of MCT1 required the manual curation of template structures.
source: The use of shallow MSAs was instrumental to obtaining structurally diverse models in most proteins, and in one case (MCT1) accurate modeling of alternative conformations also required the manual curation of template structures.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the study.

claim: The DeepMind team reportedly required templates to obtain models of LmrP in an OF conformation.
source: Indeed, whereas the DeepMind team reportedly required templates to obtain models of LmrP in an OF conformation (Jumper et al., 2021b), we found that this procedure was usually unnecessary.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the DeepMind team's report.

claim: Accurate representatives of distinct conformers were generally obtainable with exhaustive sampling and could be identified by performing PCA and selecting models at the extreme positions of PC1.
source: Accurate representatives of distinct conformers were generally obtainable with exhaustive sampling and could be identified by performing PCA and selecting models at the extreme positions of PC1.
evidence: This is a methodological conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: This approach showed limited success when applied to transporters whose structures were used to train AF2.
source: Moreover, this approach showed limited success when applied to transporters whose structures were used to train AF2, hinting at the possibility that traditional methods may still be required to capture alternative conformers (Crawley et al., 2011; Ollikainen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experiments with an inference about implications.

claim: The structural model of GPR114/ADGRG5 deposited in the AF2 database likely depicts an active conformation that diverges from the structure of the homolog GPR97.
source: The structural model deposited in the AF2 database, which likely depicts an active conformation that diverges from the structure of the homolog GPR97 (Ping et al., 2021), could be recapitulated by using deep MSAs.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with a homolog structure.

claim: The use of shallow MSAs (≤64 sequences) for GPR114/ADGRG5 yielded a range of intermediate conformations distributed across three well-separated clusters.
source: The use of shallow MSAs (≤64 sequences), by contrast, yielded a range of intermediate conformations distributed across three well-separated clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from applying the method to GPR114/ADGRG5.

claim: One cluster of GPR114/ADGRG5 models contains models with an orientation of TM6 and TM7 that fully occludes the orthosteric site and partially blocks the cytosolic pocket where G proteins bind.
source: One of these clusters contains models with an orientation of TM6 and TM7 that fully occludes the orthosteric site and partially blocks the cytosolic pocket where G proteins bind.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the models.

claim: The physiological relevance of the proposed structural movements of GPR114/ADGRG5 requires experimental validation.
source: The physiological relevance of these proposed structural movements nonetheless requires experimental validation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the need for experimental verification.

claim: AF2 can provide models to guide biophysical studies of conformationally heterogeneous membrane proteins.
source: While these results reinforce the notion that AF2 can provide models to guide biophysical studies of conformationally heterogeneous membrane proteins, they represent a methodological 'hack', rather than an explicit objective built into the algorithm's architecture.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the utility of the approach.

claim: The results represent a methodological 'hack', rather than an explicit objective built into AF2's architecture.
source: While these results reinforce the notion that AF2 can provide models to guide biophysical studies of conformationally heterogeneous membrane proteins, they represent a methodological 'hack', rather than an explicit objective built into the algorithm's architecture.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the nature of the approach.

claim: AF2, despite its accuracy, likely does not learn the energy landscapes underpinning protein folding and function.
source: Several preprints have provided evidence that AF2, despite its accuracy, likely does not learn the energy landscapes underpinning protein folding and function (Saldaño et al., 2021; Pak et al., 2021; Akdel et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to preprints.

claim: AF2 does not directly account for the lipid environment.
source: Moreover, AF2 does not directly account for the lipid environment, which has been experimentally shown to bias the conformational equilibria of membrane proteins (Martens et al., 2018; Muller et al., 2019; Immadisetty et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about AF2's limitations supported by citations.

claim: The lipid environment has been experimentally shown to bias the conformational equilibria of membrane proteins.
source: Moreover, AF2 does not directly account for the lipid environment, which has been experimentally shown to bias the conformational equilibria of membrane proteins (Martens et al., 2018; Muller et al., 2019; Immadisetty et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The exploration of the conformational space is in part a byproduct of low sequence information provided for inference.
source: As our results show, the exploration of the conformational space is in part a byproduct of low sequence information provided for inference.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The results highlight the need for further development of artificial intelligence methods capable of learning the conformational flexibility intrinsic to protein structures.
source: Ultimately, they highlight the need for further development of artificial intelligence methods capable of learning the conformational flexibility intrinsic to protein structures.
evidence: This is a forward-looking conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: All MSAs were obtained using the MMSeqs2 server.
source: First, all MSAs were obtained using the MMSeqs2 server (Steinegger and Söding, 2017), rather than the default databases.
evidence: This describes the methodology with a citation.

claim: Template search was disabled, except when explicitly performed with specific templates of interest.
source: Second, template search was disabled, except when explicitly performed with specific templates of interest (see below).
evidence: This describes the methodology.

claim: The number of recycles was set to one, rather than three by default.
source: Third, the number of recycles was set to one, rather than three by default.
evidence: This describes the methodology.

claim: Models were not refined following their prediction.
source: Finally, models were not refined following their prediction.
evidence: This describes the methodology.

claim: The study utilized all 5 neural networks when predicting structures without templates, with 10 predictions per neural network per MSA size.
source: This study utilized all 5 neural networks when predicting structures without templates, with 10 predictions per neural network per MSA size.
evidence: This describes the methodology.

claim: Residues 1–131 and 401–461 of CGRPR were omitted from modeling.
source: The following residues were omitted from modeling: 1–131 and 401–461 of CGRPR, 1–247 of FZD7, 1–175 and 492–593 of PTH1R, and 1–49 of LAT1.
evidence: This describes the methodology.

claim: MSA subsampling was carried out randomly by AF2.
source: MSA subsampling was carried out randomly by AF2, and depth values were controlled by modifying 'max_msa_clusters' and 'max_extra_msa' parameters prior to execution.
evidence: This describes the methodology.

claim: No manual intervention was carried out to fine-tune the composition of the alignments.
source: No manual intervention was carried out to fine-tune the composition of these alignments.
evidence: This describes the methodology.

claim: TM scores were calculated using TM align.
source: TM scores were calculated using TM align (Zhang and Skolnick, 2005).
evidence: This describes the methodology with a citation.

claim: PCA and RMSF calculations were carried out in CPPTRAJ.
source: PCA and RMSF calculations were carried out in CPPTRAJ (Roe and Cheatham, 2013).
evidence: This describes the methodology with a citation.

claim: Loop residues were omitted from PCA.
source: Loop residues were omitted from PCA.
evidence: This describes the methodology.
